lesson.menu_desc: Comparing two options and defending the choice out loud -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- Better, Bigger, More Stylish
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Giovanna Waltrick | Lesson 6 -- Better, Bigger, More Stylish

listenings.text: My job is to choose suppliers, which means my job is to compare. I look at three things and I look at them in this order. The price. How long the fabric lasts. And how fast they can deliver. People assume the first one decides everything, and in my experience it decides almost nothing. The cheapest supplier is rarely the best choice, because whatever I save on the price I lose later on returns from customers, and a return costs me far more than the difference. The third one surprises students the most. The most convenient supplier is not the closest one, and it is not the biggest one either. It is the one that answers the phone. If something goes wrong on a Friday afternoon, and something always goes wrong on a Friday afternoon, the supplier who picks up is worth more than the supplier who is ten percent cheaper.

I had to choose between two cities for my exchange year, and everybody had an opinion. The first one was the capital, which is bigger, more convenient and has far more to do on a Saturday. It is also much more crowded and considerably more expensive, and I would have spent half my money on rent. The second one was a smaller city that nobody outside the country has heard of. What decided it in the end was not the city at all. It was the course. The smaller one had the better programme for exactly what I wanted to study, and the bigger one had a famous name and a syllabus that did not interest me. So I went to the small one, and I do not regret the city for a second. What I do regret is not asking more people before I decided. I talked to two. I should have talked to ten.
